title: The Soup Grew on Me
scene: On a chilly evening, a friend serves cold tomato soup with warm bread. You expected something hot and hesitate to say so, but she makes room for an honest reaction. After a few spoonfuls, the unfamiliar flavor starts to appeal to you.
sceneJa: 肌寒い夜、友人が温かいパンと冷たいトマトスープを出してくれた。温かい料理を想像していたので少し戸惑うが、友人は無理に褒めなくていいと言ってくれる。何口か食べるうちに、その味がだんだん好きになっていく。

chunks.en: my friend served cold tomato soup
chunks.ja: 友人が冷たいトマトスープを出してくれた

chunks.en: It wasn't quite what I had in mind,
chunks.ja: 思い描いていたものとは少し違ったけれど

chunks.en: but I didn't want to make a fuss
chunks.ja: 大げさに騒ぎ立てたくはなかった
せっかく彼女が料理してくれたのだから
彼女は僕がためらっているのに気づいて

chunks.en: and said, 'You don't have to pretend
chunks.ja: 「無理に好きなふりをしなくても
もうひと口食べてみると
さっぱりとした酸味のある味が
だんだん好きになってきた

chunks.en: I think I like it more
chunks.ja: こっちのほうが好きかも
パンと一緒に食べるとね」と正直に伝えた

chunks.en: She passed me the last slice
chunks.ja: 彼女は最後のひと切れを渡してくれて

chunks.en: and said she'd saved some soup
chunks.ja: スープを少し取ってあると言った

chunks.en: for tomorrow, if I wanted it.
chunks.ja: 僕がよければ明日の分に、と

questions.question: Which split keeps both useful expressions intact and separates the reason?
options: It wasn't quite / what I had in mind, but I / didn't want to make a fuss after she'd cooked for us.
It wasn't quite what I had in mind, / but I didn't want to make a fuss / after she'd cooked for us.
It wasn't quite what I had / in mind, but I didn't want / to make a fuss after she'd cooked for us.
questions.explanation: 'It wasn't quite what I had in mind' gently describes unmet expectations; 'didn't want to make a fuss' expresses reluctance to complain. Keep each as a speaking unit.

questions.question: What does 'the taste started to grow on me' mean?
options: The soup became hotter as time passed.
I gradually began to like the flavor.
I had liked the soup from the first spoonful.
questions.explanation: When something grows on you, you gradually like it more than you did at first. It doesn't mean the food itself grows.

questions.question: Why does the friend say 'You don't have to pretend you love it'?
options: She is asking the guest to stop eating immediately.
She wants to prove her recipe is the best.
She is making it safe for the guest to be honest about an unfamiliar taste.
questions.explanation: The friend notices hesitation and removes social pressure. This is reassurance, not criticism.

speak: Imagine: a friend serves you an unfamiliar dish. Read: picture the chilly evening and the warm bread. Chunk: keep 'It wasn't quite what I had in mind', 'I didn't want to make a fuss', and 'It started to grow on me' together as natural units. Understand: 'not quite what I had in mind' softens disappointment; 'make a fuss' means react or complain more than needed; 'grow on me' means gradually become more appealing. Check: answer all three questions. Speak (30 seconds): describe a food, song, or place you weren't sure about at first. Say what you expected, how you reacted politely, and whether it grew on you. Try 'It wasn't quite what I had in mind', 'I didn't want to make a fuss', and 'It grew on me'. Final Read: read all six sentences smoothly without Japanese, making the guest sound hesitant at first and genuinely warmer by the end.
review: New: 'It wasn't quite what I had in mind' (想像していたものとは少し違った), 'I didn't want to make a fuss' (大げさに文句を言いたくなかった), 'It grew on me' (だんだん好きになった; in the story: 'started to grow on me'). Reuse Lesson 98 'You don't have to ...' to remove pressure about taste rather than a deadline, and Lesson 93 'For what it's worth' to offer a gentle personal opinion rather than comfort someone after a social mistake. Unlike recent museum, cat, and jazz stories, this episode explores changing tastes and making honesty comfortable. Dictionary checks: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/grow-on and https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/fuss .
